title: Photography Contract | Free Word Template
description: Free photography contract: set scope, fees, deliverables, usage rights and cancellation for photo sessions.
lead: A contract between a photographer and a client (wedding, portrait, commercial, event) covering session details, fees, deliverables, turnaround time, usage rights, deposits and cancellation.
introParagraphs: A photography contract sets expectations for both sides: what will be shot, how long the session is, how many/which photos are delivered, turnaround time, print/digital delivery, usage rights for the client, and cancellation/reschedule terms.
For weddings and commercial shoots especially, never work without a signed contract — they are expensive, one-time events and copyright matters.
bullets: Parties and event
Photographer and client names/contact; event/session type (wedding, portrait, commercial, event); date, start time and location.
Scope and deliverables
Hours of coverage, second shooter/assistant included, number of edited photos delivered, turnaround time, delivery method (gallery/USB), and products included (albums, prints).
Fees and payment
Total fee, deposit/retainer amount and due date, final payment deadline, travel fees, extra hours rate, and payment methods.
Usage rights and copyright
Client gets personal/non-commercial usage license; photographer retains copyright and portfolio/marketing rights unless commercial usage is purchased; commercial shoots spell out license scope.
Cancellation, reschedule and liability
Deposit refundability, reschedule policy, force majeure, photographer backup plan if unable to attend, limitation of liability, and model release if applicable.
howTo: Lock the date with a retainer
Collect a non-refundable retainer (typically 25-50%) to reserve the date.
Spell out deliverables precisely
State approximate number of edited images, delivery format, and turnaround time (e.g. 4-6 weeks for weddings).
Clarify usage rights
Personal use for clients; commercial license separately. Include portfolio rights for photographer.
Address what if you cannot shoot
Include a substitute-photographer clause for illness/emergency and a refund limit.
Have client sign before the shoot
Do not show up to shoot without a signed contract and paid retainer.
faq: Who owns the photos?
The photographer automatically owns copyright in most countries; the client receives a license to use them. Commercial buyouts transfer specific rights.
Are deposits refundable?
Retainers are usually non-refundable if the client cancels close to the date (because you turned down other work).
Do I need a model release?
If you plan to use identifiable people photos in portfolio/marketing, yes — particularly for commercial use.
What if the client wants RAW files?
This is a negotiable business choice — many photographers do not provide RAWs; state the policy in the contract.
What happens if it rains?
For outdoor sessions include a weather/reschedule backup plan.

title: Graphic Design Contract | Free Word Template
description: Free graphic design contract: set scope, deliverables, revisions, fees, IP rights and kill fees for design work.
lead: A contract between a graphic designer and client defining design scope, deliverables, revision rounds, fees, payment schedule, IP ownership and kill-fee terms.
introParagraphs: A graphic design contract defines what the designer will deliver (logo, brand identity, website mockups, marketing materials), the number of included revision rounds, fees and payment milestones, and who owns the final IP when payment is complete.
Killer clauses: revision limits (preventing endless iterations), kill fees (if the client cancels mid-project), and clear IP transfer on final payment.
bullets: Parties and project
Designer name/business; client name; project name/brief; start date and estimated completion date.
Scope and deliverables
Specific list of deliverables (logo variations, brand guide, brochure, social assets), file formats (AI, EPS, PDF, PNG, JPG), and sizes/dimensions.
Revisions and approvals
Number of included revision rounds, what counts as a revision vs new scope, feedback turnaround expectations, and approval process for final deliverables.
Fees and payment
Total fee (flat, hourly), deposit/retainer (typically 50%), milestone payments, late fees, expenses (fonts, stock photos, printing), and payment methods.
IP, kill fee and credit
Copyright transfers to client on final payment; designer retains portfolio rights and right of credit; kill fee if client cancels mid-project; client retains rights to their provided materials.
howTo: Attach the brief
Attach a creative brief/spec as an exhibit — vague scope kills design projects.
Limit revision rounds
Include 2-3 rounds; charge hourly for additional rounds to keep scope controlled.
Tie IP transfer to final payment
Copyright only transfers when final invoice is paid — protects you from non-payment.
Agree on kill fees
If the client cancels mid-project, a kill fee (e.g. 50% of remaining or % of work completed) compensates work done.
Clarify stock assets
State who pays for stock photos, fonts, templates and third-party assets, and who holds their licenses.
related: For larger engagements with multiple deliverables.
faq: Who owns the design?
Usually the client on final payment; designer retains portfolio/moral rights and rights to unused concepts.
Can I use fonts commercially?
License fonts properly — the contract should state who buys the license (usually client).
How many revisions are normal?
2-3 rounds per deliverable is standard; additional rounds billed hourly.
What if the client hates the work?
A clear feedback/approval process plus revision rounds protects both sides; some designers offer a redo within limits.
Do I need a contract for small projects?
Yes — even a short contract prevents the 'just one more tweak' cycle and non-payment.

title: Web Design Contract | Free Word Template
description: Free web design contract: set scope, pages, revisions, fees, launch terms and post-launch support for websites.
lead: A contract between a web designer/developer and a client covering design scope, number of pages, CMS/platform, revisions, hosting/domain responsibilities, fees, launch and post-launch support.
introParagraphs: A web design contract defines what website the designer will build, what platform/CMS it will use, how many pages/templates, who provides content, what browsers/devices it supports, the launch process, and what post-launch support is included.
Web projects are prone to scope creep (extra features, content delays). Clear revision rounds, content deadlines and change-order procedures are essential.
bullets: Parties and project
Designer/developer name/business; client name; project description/scope; start date and estimated launch date.
Scope and deliverables
Number of pages/templates, platform (WordPress, Webflow, custom), key features (contact form, e-commerce, blog), design rounds, browser/device support, and whether content migration is included.
Client responsibilities
Content copy, images and branding assets by deadlines, feedback turnaround, domain/hosting setup, and point of contact.
Fees and payment
Total project fee, deposit (e.g. 50%), milestone payments (design approval, development, launch), late fees, and extra-work/change-order rates.
Launch, support and IP
Launch date, client training/walkthrough, post-launch support period (e.g. 30 days bug fixes), hosting/maintenance terms, IP transfer on final payment, and designer portfolio rights.
howTo: Define scope tightly
List specific pages, templates and features; anything not listed is out of scope.
Set content deadlines
Client-delayed content is the #1 reason web projects slip — state who provides what by when, and delays push launch.
Limit revisions
Include 2-3 rounds of design revisions and change-order rate for extra features.
Specify browser/device support
Name supported browsers (evergreen) and breakpoint targets (desktop, tablet, mobile); you cannot support every legacy browser.
Clarify post-launch
Include 30 days bug fixes; ongoing maintenance/hosting is a separate retainer or client responsibility.
related: For design assets used on the site.
Ongoing marketing that may accompany a new site.
Master services agreement for broader engagements.
faq: Who owns the website?
Client owns the final design and content on final payment; designer retains rights to code libraries/portfolio unless work-for-hire.
Do I provide hosting?
Choose a clear policy — either you arrange hosting (with a recurring fee) or the client signs up for their own account.
Are plugins/fonts included?
State who pays for premium themes/plugins/fonts and who holds the licenses.
What about SEO?
Specify whether basic on-page SEO is included or a separate service.
What if the client does not provide content?
Include a clause that content delays push the timeline and may incur a project-pause fee.

title: Freelance Writing Contract | Free Word Template
description: Free freelance writing contract: set scope, word count, revisions, pay, rights and deadlines for writing work.
lead: A contract between a freelance writer and client covering scope (articles, copy, books), word count, revisions, deadlines, payment terms, rights purchased and kill fees.
introParagraphs: A freelance writing contract defines what the writer will produce (article, blog post, copy, white paper, book), word count or deliverable, deadline, number of revisions, rate (per word, per project, or hourly), and what rights the client is buying (first rights, all rights, web rights, etc.).

Without a contract, scope creep ('can you just add a section?') and payment delays are common. Kill fees are especially important for writing because invested time is hard to recover if the client cancels.
bullets: Writer and client
Writer name; client/publication name and contact; project title/brief reference.
Deliverables
What will be written (article, blog post series, copy deck, e-book), approximate word count, format (Google Doc, Word, Markdown), tone and style guidance.
Deadlines and revisions
Draft deadline, revisions included (typically 1-2 rounds), feedback turnaround time by client, and publication date/embargo rules.
Payment terms
Rate (per word, per project, hourly), total fee, deposit, payment due date (on delivery, net 15/30), kill fee if cancelled mid-project, and invoice process.
Rights and credit
Rights purchased (first North American serial, all rights, exclusive web rights, etc.), whether the writer gets a byline, portfolio rights, and reprint rights.
howTo: Attach the brief
Attach a detailed brief describing topic, audience, tone, keywords, and word count.
State rights clearly
Writers often grant specific rights (e.g. first publication rights for X months), not all rights forever; price accordingly.
Include a kill fee
If the client cancels after work starts, pay a % of the fee (25-100% depending on stage).
Set revision limits
1-2 rounds of revisions included; major rewrites are billed extra.
Define payment schedule
Deposit up front, remainder on delivery (or on publication for publications); specify late fees.
related: Master contract for ongoing freelance work.
For content that pairs with design.
For coaching services (a different kind of freelance).
faq: What rights am I selling?
It depends on the deal: all rights/work-for-hire means you cannot reuse it; first rights means they publish first then rights revert; exclusive rights means only they can publish during a period.
Do freelance writers get credit?
Byline is common for editorial content; ghostwriting means no byline (charge more).
Is a deposit required?
For new clients always (25-50%); for established publications payment on delivery/acceptance is standard.
What if they reject the work?
Define in the contract whether rewrites are included or if a kill fee applies.
Can I use the work in my portfolio?
Negotiate portfolio rights in the contract — you want to be able to show published work.

title: Video Production Contract | Free Word Template
description: Free video production contract: set scope, deliverables, revisions, licensing, fees and cancellation for video projects.
lead: A contract between a video producer/videographer and client covering the concept, shoot days, deliverables (edit length, formats), revision rounds, licensing of footage/music, fees and cancellation terms.
introParagraphs: A video production contract covers pre-production (script, planning), production (shoot days, crew, locations, talent) and post-production (editing, revisions, color grading, audio mixing, delivery formats).
Video projects are expensive to crew and shoot — lock scope, shoot dates, revision rounds, music licensing and deliverables clearly to avoid massive scope creep.
bullets: Producer and client
Production company/DP name; client name and contact; project title/concept; estimated production and delivery dates.
Scope and deliverables
Video concept and length (e.g. 3 minute brand film + 30s cutdown), shoot days/locations, crew included (DP, sound, gaffer), number of edited versions, delivery formats (4K, 1080p, social cuts).
Production responsibilities
Client provides: talent, locations, access, approvals. Producer provides: crew, gear, basic editing. Stated turnaround for first cut and final delivery.
Fees, expenses and revisions

Total production fee, deposit (typically 50%), payment milestones, included revision rounds (typically 2-3), rate for extra revisions/shoot days, and pass-through expenses (travel, talent, location permits, stock/music licensing).
Licensing, cancellation and liability

Usage rights/license for the final video (web, broadcast, in-perpetuity or time-limited); music/stock licensing; cancellation/reschedule terms; weather backup; liability caps; and producer portfolio rights.
howTo: Sign off on the script/storyboard
Pre-production is where you prevent costly reshoots — get script and storyboard approved before shooting.
Lock shoot dates
Confirm crew/location/talent availability and book with deposits.
Limit revision rounds
2-3 rounds of edits is typical; extra rounds billed hourly or per day.
Clarify music licensing
State who pays for licensed music; royalty-free music has terms that must be respected.
Include a cancellation schedule
Cancellations within X days of shoot may forfeit the deposit; rescheduling weather dependent shoots.
related: Stills equivalent; sometimes bundled with video.
Video is often a vendor at events.
faq: Who owns raw footage?
Production company typically owns raw footage unless the contract says otherwise; client receives the final edited video. Raw footage can be purchased separately.
Is music included?
Specify who pays for stock/licensed music and whether commercial/broadcast rights are included.
Can the client demand unlimited edits?
Include a revision cap (2-3 rounds); extra revisions are billed at an hourly/day rate.
Do talent/location releases come with the project?
Producer typically coordinates releases for talent/location they arrange; client is responsible for releases for their own employees/locations.
What if weather ruins an outdoor shoot?
Include a weather day/reschedule clause — often at client cost or shared.
